summary:
Salta Province stands under Argentina's national framework. Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention. Reuters reported the ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents.

Trans activists interviewed by the Washington Blade in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation. They reported that the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated, that trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, were dismissed, and that the quota is no longer being implemented. The 2012 Gender Identity Law and the 'X' marker on the national identity document, available since 2021, remain formally in force but are no longer guaranteed in practice, activists said.

Violence reached a documented peak in 2025. Agencia Presentes reported on 19 March 2026 that the national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 attacks against LGBT+ people over the year, a rise of 62% year-on-year and the worst of the observatory's ten recorded years, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 of 227. Physical violence against bodily integrity made up 64.8% of cases, 147. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, with beatings the main modality. The observatory attributes the surge to the national government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people and to hate discourse. The same period saw DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatments.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so that the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

No Salta-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors. Interior provinces without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real, so the absence of provincial data reflects documentation capacity rather than demonstrated safety.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's formal position and its reported practice have diverged. The country holds one of the world's most permissive gender-recognition statutes and the region's first marriage-equality law, yet the national hate-crime tally for 2025 was the highest in ten years of recording and Outright International's March 2026 overview assesses gender recognition negatively, marking deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

The pattern of harm is concentrated on trans women and travestis, who were 62.5% of recorded victims in 2025, and the perpetrators named most often are security-force personnel operating in public space. Visitors should read the national statistics as the visible portion of a record kept mainly by Buenos Aires-based organisations; provinces with no local observatory contribute little to the count.

Activists interviewed in April 2025 linked the deterioration directly to the national government's policy direction, describing the elimination of the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and the non-implementation of the Trans Labor Quota Law as the backdrop to a chaotic and desperate situation, and the observatory likewise attributes the 2025 surge to official 'cultural battle' rhetoric.
